title_en: David Booth: ‘The Markets Work Well for Everybody, Not Just the Insiders’
title_zh: David Booth：'市场为每个人良好运转，而不只是内部人士'
subtitle_zh: Dimensional 创始人 David Booth 谈数据、有效市场假说（EMH）与投资的科学：信任市场，保持冷静，长期在场。
description: David Booth: ‘The Markets Work Well for Everybody, Not Just the Insiders’

turns.en: Welcome to the Longview. I'm Ben Johnson, Head of Client Solutions with Morningstar. And I'm Amy Arnott, Portfolio Strategist for Morningstar.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 The Long View。我是 Ben Johnson，Morningstar 客户解决方案主管。我是 Amy Arnott，Morningstar 组合策略师。

turns.en: Today's guest on the Longview is David Booth. David is a repeat guest, the founder of Dimensional Fund Advisors, and has just released a new book titled, Stay Calm, Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life.
turns.zh: 本期 The Long View 的嘉宾是 David Booth。David 是老客人了，他是 Dimensional Fund Advisors 的创始人，刚刚出版了一本新书《Stay Calm, Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life》。

turns.en: Amy, we had such a terrific conversation with David. And there are almost too many highlights for me to choose from. So I'm going to really call out what I thought was one of the interesting through lines, which really centered on data.
turns.zh: Amy，我们和大卫的这场对话实在太精彩，亮点多到我几乎无从取舍。所以我只想拎出一条我觉得特别有意思的主线，它其实是围绕数据的。

turns.en: And at one point, David shared with us, without data, people are just arguing beliefs. And there was so much time within our industry where investors really were in a data desert.
turns.zh: 大卫在节目里跟我们说过：没有数据，人们就只是在争论各自的信念。在我们这个行业里，有相当长的时间，投资者其实都身处数据的荒漠。

turns.en: And really that foundational layer was critical to everything that David, his colleagues at Dimensional and so many others around the broader investing industry, have ultimately brought to bear for the benefit of so many investors over the years who once may have felt like outsiders and are now very much inside and benefiting from decades worth of research and work in a way that they couldn't have just without that data foundation.
turns.zh: 而那块数据地基，对大卫、对 Dimensional 的同事们、对整个投资行业里的无数人来说都至关重要——正是这一切，让一代代曾经自视为局外人的投资者，如今真正成了局内人，受益于几十年的研究与积累；而没有那层数据基础，这一切都无从谈起。

turns.en: So the through line of data is mundane as it seems today in 2026 really stood out to me. Yeah, Ben, I thought that was a really interesting point too.
turns.zh: 所以说，'数据'这条主线，在 2026 年的今天看来如此稀松平常，反而格外让我印象深刻。是啊 Ben，我也觉得那一点特别有意思。

turns.en: And I really love David's comments about how having access to a more complete data set can really help provide a sense of calmness and reassurance for investors, even in an uncertain environment.
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢大卫说的：能接触到更完整的数据集，能给投资者一种镇定和宽慰，哪怕环境依旧充满不确定。

turns.en: And another highlight for me, stay tuned to find out more about Jean Fama's favorite Swedish pop group. Oh, no. Now that we've got people on the edge of their seats, Amy, without further ado, let's dig in with David.
turns.zh: 我的另一个亮点是：请听下去，看看 Gene Fama 最喜欢的瑞典流行乐队是谁。哦不。好了，既然大家都已经坐不住了，Amy，事不宜迟，我们这就和大卫开聊。

turns.en: David, welcome back to the long view. Thank you so much for joining Amy and I today. Thanks for having me. David, the occasion for you coming back to the podcast is that you've just published a new book, Stay Calm, Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life.
turns.zh: David，欢迎回到 The Long View，非常感谢你今天加入我和 Amy 的对话。谢谢邀请。David，你这次重返节目的由头，是你刚出了新书《Stay Calm, Learn to Embrace Uncertainty in Investing and Life》。

turns.en: And I want to start with the life bit of that, notably in the book you describe yourself as a bit of an outsider having been born in Garnet, Kansas, being Kansas born and bred.
turns.zh: 我想先从书名里'生活'那部分聊起。你在书里形容自己算是个局外人——出生在堪萨斯州的 Garnett，土生土长的堪萨斯人。

turns.en: How did that ultimately sort of become part of the way that you view the world and by extension in your career form the way that you viewed markets investing in a way that fundamentally was different from and in many ways has reshaped what were conventional Wall Street norms?
turns.zh: 这种背景最终如何成了你看世界的方式，又延伸到你的职业生涯里，塑造了你对市场和投资的看法——一种从根本上与众不同、并在很多方面重塑了华尔街传统规范的看法？

turns.en: Well, I think a lot of people view themselves as being outsiders and my parents were kind of that way. And they thought that, well, it's the insiders that make all the money.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想很多人都会自视为局外人，我父母就是那样。他们会觉得，赚钱的都是内部人士。

turns.en: So I'm not going to invest because the insiders will just take advantage of me. That's kind of a, unfortunately, a view a lot of people have.
turns.zh: 所以我才不投资，内部人士只会占我便宜。不幸的是，这恰恰是很多人真实的想法。

turns.en: And that's where the science has really helped people a lot, the development of financial science in the 60s and 70s. The conclusion is that the markets work well for everybody, not just the insiders.
turns.zh: 而科学真正帮到大大的地方就在这里——60、70 年代金融科学的发展。结论是：市场运转得很好，为每个人服务，而不只是内部人士。

turns.en: In fact, the insiders seem to have a rough time doing as well as the market. It's actually the outsiders that should feel good about all this academic research and so forth. Because today you can buy market portfolios very easily.
turns.zh: 事实上，内部人士似乎反而更难做得像市场那样好。真正该对这些学术研究感到振奋的，恰恰是局外人。因为今天你可以非常轻松地买到市场组合。

turns.en: You can buy the market. And that seems to be about as well as the pros do. Now, personally, also being an outsider coming in, going to the University of Chicago in the PhD program in the late 60s, it was an incredibly stimulating time.
turns.zh: 你可以买下整个市场，而表现和专业人士差不多好。再说我个人，也是作为局外人走进来的：60 年代末去芝加哥大学读博士项目，那真是一段令人振奋的时光。

turns.en: And the field of finance was changing. And you could characterize these academics themselves as being outsiders to the mainstream Wall Street crowd.
turns.zh: 当时金融这个学科正在巨变。而那些学者本身，其实也可以视为主流华尔街圈子的局外人。

turns.en: In fact, all this research really challenged kind of the prevailing point of view of Wall Street in the 60s and 70s and led to this. This revolution in finance that's really helped people tremendously, you know, the fees, the result of this research and the applications, his fees are much lower.
turns.zh: 事实上，所有这些研究都在挑战 60、70 年代华尔街的主流观念，引发了那场金融革命，真的极大帮助了人们。你看，正是这些研究和应用的成果，费用变得低得多了。

turns.en: So that's got to help. And then portfolios are better designed and so forth. All of that comes from having these academics that are kind of outsiders, you know, examining the data.
turns.zh: 这本身当然有帮助。然后组合设计得更好，如此等等。这一切都源于这些学者——某种意义上他们也是局外人——在那儿审视数据。

turns.en: For 1960, researchers really didn't have the data to analyze a lot of the claims of people on Wall Street. That all changed in the 60s and without an explosion of research.
turns.zh: 回到 1960 年，研究者其实没有数据去检验华尔街人们的那些说法。这一切在 60 年代变了，研究呈现爆发式增长。

turns.en: And along with that came some complicated ideas, but there also came a lot of great insights that are really helpful to everybody. David, I want to ask a quick follow up there.
turns.zh: 随之而来有一些复杂的概念，但也带来了大量对每个人都真正有用的洞见。David，我想在这儿快速追问一句。

turns.en: You mentioned, you know, just something as simple as the notion that up until that period of time hadn't been documented shows that, you know, markets, stock markets deliver roughly 10% annual returns.
turns.zh: 你提到，比如再简单不过的一件事——在那之前，从来没有人记录并证明过：股票市场大致能带来约 10% 的年化回报。

turns.en: Why was that such, you know, now in sort of looking the review mirror seems awfully mundane and, you know, has just, I think, become internalized by a lot of investors?
turns.zh: 为什么这在当时那么——如今在后视镜里看似乎稀松平常，早已被很多投资者内化了——

turns.en: Why was that such a sort of seminal moment in hindsight, the fact that, you know, these markets that work so well for so many and have now for decades, it was kind of a discovery.
turns.zh: 为什么以事后之明看，那是一个开创性的时刻？这些为那么多人良好运转的市场，几十年来一直如此，可在当时其实是一项发现。

turns.en: It feels like, you know, in the world of finance and investing, like almost the equivalent of, like, the discovery of fire in my mind. Well, I mean, in some ways, it is similar, see, because when you don't have data and people are making all kinds of claims, you know, that's when people really did feel like outsiders, you know, and probably they could be taken advantage of because you didn't have a data to show them any other way.
turns.zh: 在金融和投资的世界里，这几乎相当于'火的发现'。嗯，我觉得某些意义上确实如此。因为在没有数据、人人各说各话的年代，人们真的觉得自己是局外人，而且很可能被人占便宜——因为你没有数据去告诉他们还有另一种真相。

turns.en: And then with the data, all of a sudden, you know, people could feel comfortable that markets work the way that we hoped they would, you know, stocks do better than bonds with the long haul and so forth.
turns.zh: 而有了数据之后，人们突然可以安心了：市场确实如我们所期望的那样运转——长期看股票确实好于债券，等等。

turns.en: And over the long haul, stocks have about a 10% return. That sounds like a fair deal. I mean, you're covering now we have 100 years of data.
turns.zh: 长期下来股票大约 10% 的回报，听起来是一笔公道的交易。如今我们已经覆盖了一百年的数据。

turns.en: And now at Morningstar, you have 100 years of data, research quality. That covers a wide range of scenarios, you know, if you as a researcher, you want a good test sample, right?
turns.zh: 而在 Morningstar，你们现在也有了这一百年研究质量的数据，覆盖各种情形。做研究嘛，你当然想要一个好的测试样本，对吧？

turns.en: Well, how about the last 100 years of your examining stock and bond returns? You know, it covers a historically great depression, it goes through World War II, Korean War, you know, periods of high inflation, the Great Recession, so on and so forth.
turns.zh: 那还有什么比'检验过去一百年的股债回报'更好的呢？这中间有大萧条、二战、朝鲜战争、高通胀时期、大衰退，等等。

turns.en: If you're looking for a test period, the last 100 years is about as good as you're going to come up with. And through all of that, 10% a year, which is part of the reason that I wrote the book as well.
turns.zh: 要找一段测试期，过去一百年差不多是你所能找到的最好的了。而穿越这一切，年化依然是 10%——这也是我写那本书的原因之一。

turns.en: You know, a lot of people have anxiety about markets today, some seems elevated this year more than some other years. And what we want to do is if people understood better about how markets work, I think they'd be a more optimistic about investing and feel more confident they can have a good investment experience long term.
turns.zh: 我在芝加哥学到的最重要的东西——除了别的那些——就是：跟人对话时，如果没有数据，你们就只是在争论各自的信念，而什么信念你都可以有。

turns.en: And the main thing I learned from Chicago, well, none of the many things was just, you know, if you're having conversations with people, if you don't have data, you're just arguing beliefs, and you can believe anything.
turns.zh: 你知道，很多人如今对市场有焦虑，有些年份显得比别的年份更高。我们想做的是：如果人们更懂市场如何运作，我想他们会对投资更乐观，也更有信心长期拥有良好的投资体验。

turns.en: I mean, so the data was revolutionary. Right. And I was going to say, when you have access to data, I think that can help you stay calm. You know, if there's a big decline in the market, you realize that's not unusual, and things usually do turn around or always turn around eventually.
turns.zh: 可以说，数据带来了一场革命。对。我还想说：当你手上有数据，我觉得它能帮你保持冷静。市场大跌时，你明白那并不罕见，事情通常都会好转，或者说迟早总会好转。

turns.en: Well, that's one of the things that then we're going to the last dozen years or so is just basically drawing parallels to what goes on in investing with what goes on in life and this whole notion of dealing with uncertainty.
turns.zh: 嗯，这正是我过去十几年反复在谈的——把投资里发生的事和人生里发生的事做类比，也就是这整套关于应对不确定性的理念。

turns.en: First thing I try to talk to people about is just, you know, uncertainty creates opportunity. And that sounds strange at first. But if there were no uncertainty, you know, it'd probably been difficult for you to progress in life.
turns.zh: 我跟人交流的第一件事就是：不确定性创造机会。这乍听有点怪。但如果没有不确定性，你的人生恐怕也很难有进步。

turns.en: And the same thing is true in investing. If there were no uncertainty, then everything's riskless and all investments would have the riskless rate of return.
turns.zh: 投资也一样。如果没有不确定性，那所有东西都是无风险的，所有投资都只会拿到无风险收益率。

turns.en: So it's the uncertainty that creates opportunity. And once you get people comfortable with that, then you say, so in reality, what it's about is managing uncertainty, not totally eliminating uncertainty.
turns.zh: 所以正是不确定性创造了机会。等人们对此坦然了，你再说：所以真正要做的，是管理不确定性，而不是彻底消除不确定性。

turns.en: And with that, then you can start to figure out how to develop an overall investment plan. So as you mentioned, you were a grad student at the University of Chicago in the late 1960s, which was sort of the epicenter of this big revolution in finance that was going on.
turns.zh: 有了这个，你就可以开始制定整体的投资计划了。——说到这儿，你 60 年代末在芝加哥大学读研究生，那正是这场金融大革命的中心。

turns.en: And you sat in Professor Eugene Fama's class and learned about the efficient markets hypothesis. What was it like learning from Fama? And when did it sort of click for you that markets might be more efficient than most people believed?
turns.zh: 你坐在 Eugene Fama 教授的课堂上，学习了有效市场假说（Efficient Market Hypothesis，EMH）。师从 Fama 是什么感觉？什么时候开始，你意识到市场可能比大多数人相信的更有效？

turns.en: Well, basically the first day of class, he kind of outlines his view of markets and how they work and go, that makes sense to me. I mean, my parents never invested.
turns.zh: 基本上开学第一天，他就勾勒出他对市场及其运作方式的看法。我想，这说得通。我父母从来没投资过，

turns.en: I had no experience in investing. I go, that makes so much sense. It wasn't until later I realized what an unusual opinion that was. And it was more than just Fama.
turns.zh: 我对投资毫无经验，我就觉得：这太有道理了。后来我才意识到，这观点有多不寻常。而且不只是 Fama，

turns.en: It was the finance faculty there who were really amazing and being able to work with and present papers to them and then see their research as it was coming out.
turns.zh: 那里的整个金融系教授都太出色了。能和他们共事、向他们提交论文、第一时间读到他们正在出炉的研究，

turns.en: It was incredibly stimulating. And this was back before any of them had gotten Nobel Prize in economics. And a number of them went on to become Nobel laureates.
turns.zh: 那真是无比振奋。那还是在他们任何一位获得诺贝尔经济学奖之前。他们当中好几位后来都成了诺奖得主。

turns.en: In fact, other people I worked with way back then, I mean, three of them got Nobel Prizes. And then our mutual fund board has those in addition to the Merton Miller and Myron Scholes, and they've added Bob Merton and Doug Diamond over time.
turns.zh: 事实上，当年与我共事的人里就有三位拿了诺奖。我们共同基金的董事会里，除了 Merton Miller 和 Myron Scholes，后来又陆续加入了 Bob Merton 和 Doug Diamond。

turns.en: So in total, we've worked with five Nobel laureates. And these are all young, bright people doing great research at the time. And if you could read the research, you could see it was explosive and incredibly important, which is eventually what I figured out was something that turned out to be good for me and good for the business school.
turns.zh: 加起来我们一共共事过五位诺奖得主。当年那都是一群聪明的年轻人，做着顶尖的研究。只要能读懂那些论文，就会知道那是爆发式的、极其重要的——这最后成了对我和对商学院都好的事。

turns.en: I realized I probably was better off trying to apply the ideas and letting people like Fama and Merton Miller and Myron Scholes develop the great ideas.
turns.zh: 我意识到，我大概更适合去做应用这些想法的人，把发展伟大思想的事留给 Fama、Merton Miller、Myron Scholes 他们。

turns.en: And so that's how history unfolded, and these are still good friends. Any other people I studied with, we were all young back then. Now we're all really old, but it's been a great career.
turns.zh: 历史就是这么展开的，而这些至今仍是好朋友。当年一起求学的其他人也一样，那时都年轻，现在都很老了，但那真是一段精彩的职业生涯。

turns.en: One of the anecdotes I really loved in the book was when you wrote about how you threw a party for Eugene Fama at the ABBA Museum in Stockholm, Sweden in celebration of his Nobel Prize.
turns.zh: 书里我特别喜欢一段轶事：你写到如何在斯德哥尔摩的 ABBA 博物馆给 Eugene Fama 办了一场派对，庆祝他获诺贝尔奖。

turns.en: What was that like? Well, it's kind of a University of Chicago story. I'd been to the Nobel ceremony when Myron Scholes and Bob Merton got their Nobel Prize and saw how the whole thing worked, and it's like a week-long celebration.
turns.zh: 那是什么体验？嗯，这算是个芝加哥大学的故事。Myron Scholes 和 Bob Merton 领奖时我去过一次，知道整套流程是怎么回事——那是一整周的庆典。

turns.en: They don't give these Nobel laureates much time on their own. So they had two free nights, and Eugene Fama invited me to go with him. They give him a certain number of tickets.
turns.zh: 诺奖得主几乎没什么自己的时间。但他们有两个空闲的夜晚，Eugene Fama 邀我同行，官方会分给他一些票。

turns.en: Well, in addition, because Eugene has four kids and a number of grandkids, he only had two tickets left for friends, so his long-term colleague in French and I invited us to join him.
turns.zh: 而且因为 Eugene 有四个孩子、不少孙辈，留给朋友的票只剩两张，于是他的长期同事 Ken French 和我，受邀和他一起过去。

turns.en: I said, okay, but I know how this works, Gene, and I don't think you're going to do it a good job of planning a party. So let me plan those two free nights.
turns.zh: 我跟 Gene 说：行，但我懂这个流程，你怕是不太会安排派对，那两个空闲的夜晚让我来操办吧。

turns.en: And so I called up the ABBA Museum. Stockholm has an ABBA Museum. I said, I'd like to rent the museum out tonight for a party. They go, well, we don't do that.
turns.zh: 于是我打电话给 ABBA 博物馆——斯德哥尔摩有个 ABBA 博物馆——我说我想今晚把博物馆包下来办派对。他们说：我们不接这种场。

turns.en: I go, Nobel this, Nobel that. Eventually, I wore them down and said, okay, well, we'll rent you the museum. So we had a dinner with our little group, you know, Gene's kids and grandkids and Ken French and me and had dinner at the museum.
turns.zh: 我就拿'这可是诺贝尔奖'说事，最后磨下来了：好吧，博物馆租给你们。于是我们一小拨人——Gene 的孩子和孙辈、Ken French 和我——在博物馆里吃了晚饭。

turns.en: And then afterwards, have the tour of the museum. And one part of the tour was really kind of cool. They had this platform, kind of with a microphone and a scrim behind them with all the four ABBA singers.
turns.zh: 饭后参观了博物馆。其中一段特别有意思。他们有个小舞台，配着麦克风，背景幕布上是 ABBA 四位歌手。

turns.en: And Gene's kids are incredibly talented, and so everybody's fighting for time at the mic, you know, singing ABBA songs, you know, in the background.
turns.zh: 而 Gene 的孩子们才华横溢，大家都争先恐后地挤到麦克风前唱歌，背景里放着 ABBA 的歌。

turns.en: So they would lip-sing, I guess. So is it going on? And it's really just a lot of fun. And I looked over at Gene and, you know, Gene is just a lovely human being and a great mentor of mine and a great friend.
turns.zh: 所以大概是假唱对口型吧。现场好不热闹。我看向 Gene——Gene 是个非常可爱的人，是我的良师益友，也是我的好朋友。

turns.en: And I wouldn't characterize him as a party animal. And I look at him and you could see the kind of the smile on his face. And he was really enjoying this.
turns.zh: 我可不会把他形容成派对动物。但我看着他，能看出他脸上的笑意。他真的十分享受。

turns.en: And kind of, I sense even more is all this, say, 50 years of work, they put in all this research and, you know, this was kind of his reward.
turns.zh: 我甚至更能感觉到：这一切，大家投入了差不多 50 年的研究，这大概就是给他的犒赏。

turns.en: And he was really enjoying it. So it made me feel good. What an incredible moment, the meeting of your father, the efficient markets hypothesis with, you know, dancing queen in real time.
turns.zh: 他真的很享受，这让我心里也暖暖的。多么不可思议的时刻——'有效市场假说'的父亲，现场邂逅《Dancing Queen》。

turns.en: I can only imagine. And you do such a good job of describing it, David. I'm curious, you know, when you look back at now and you've effectively bookended 50 years worth of work that, you know, I think still to this day feels revolutionary.
turns.zh: 我光是想想都觉得美妙。你把这一切描述得太好了，David。我很好奇：如今你几乎用一本书为 50 年的工作画上了句点，而这些工作到今天依然让人觉得是革命性的。

turns.en: But when you think back to, you know, the time in the 60s when Gene first published his work on the efficient markets hypothesis, did it feel even more revolutionary in that moment?
turns.zh: 可回想 60 年代 Gene 第一次发表有效市场假说研究的那个当下，会不会觉得更是石破天惊？

turns.en: And, you know, if yes or no, why or why not? Well, no, it's maybe a way to describe it, the feeling I had was, you know, this year has been kind of a big event year, you know, coming out with a book.
turns.zh: 是也好，不是也好，为什么？嗯，也许这么说吧。我的感受是，今年算是我人生里大事频出的一年：出了新书。

turns.en: We had our 45th anniversary. We crossed a trillion dollars in assets under management. And it's been a time for me to sit back and reflect on my 57 years in the business.
turns.zh: 我们迎来 45 周年，资产管理规模突破了一万亿美元。这让我有机会静下来，回望自己在这个行业里的 57 年。

turns.en: And all the good memories and the good times, you know, you kind of overlook kind of a lot of the tough times and the anxiety and focus on what's really been accomplished.
turns.zh: 所有那些美好的回忆和顺遂的时刻——你会不太去在意那些艰难和焦虑，而专注于真正做成的事。

turns.en: And I think going back to that, you know, that habit of music, I think what I got at Kalimsov was Gene really kind of internalizing all the good stuff that had happened.
turns.zh: 回到那个音乐的时刻，我想那晚 Gene 是真的在把这一切美好内化于心。

turns.en: And I'm thrilled to be able to share that with him and his family. And you have to understand it's, I think a lot of us take a lot of pride in what's happened in the last 57 years or 60 years with all this research.
turns.zh: 我很高兴能和他、和他的家人分享这一切。你要明白，过去 57 年、60 年这一切研究，我想我们很多人都深感自豪。

turns.en: It's made investing in public markets easily accessible for everybody. There's no excuse not to invest and there's no excuse for not being optimistic that you can have a good investment experience.
turns.zh: 它让投资公开市场变得对每个人唾手可得。不投资没有任何借口，也没有理由不对'拥有良好投资体验'保持乐观。

turns.en: You got to feel good about that. So you write that about 10 or 12 years ago, you realized that if you wanted more people to know about DFA's approach to investing, you needed to change how you talked about investing to get more people to kind of understand and have conversations around it.
turns.zh: 你该为此感到高兴。——书里你写到，大约 10 到 12 年前你意识到：想让更多人了解 DFA 的投资之道，就得换一种谈论投资的方式，让更多人听懂、愿意聊起它。

turns.en: So you've been having meetings every week with what you call the Tuesday group, which is a group of about 10 people, including Senator Bill Bradley, as well as Karen Dolan, who's a former Morningstar employee.
turns.zh: 于是你每周都和一个你称为'周二小组'的团体开会——大约 10 个人，包括前参议员 Bill Bradley，还有曾在 Morningstar 任职的 Karen Dolan。

turns.en: And I'm curious, how did those meetings help shape your approach to writing this book? Well, I mean, I think communication is really, nobody has a monopoly on how to do it.
turns.zh: 我很好奇：这些会议如何塑造了你写这本书的方式？嗯，我觉得沟通这件事，谁都没有垄断权。

turns.en: And it was so important for me to be able to talk to the average person. I'm steeped in quantitative methods. And while those methods are useful in the cornerstone of the firm, in terms of talking to people, it's kind of getting away.
turns.zh: 对我而言，能和平时的普通人对话太重要了。我浸淫量化多年，那些方法是公司的基石，但和人聊天时，你得从那套东西里跳出来。

turns.en: So how can we talk to people and have them relate to what has really gone on with all this academic research? And so the format I use now is that, first off, I start talking to people, what do you think of as true wealth?
turns.zh: 那么，我们怎么才能和人对话，让他们对这一切学术研究的真义产生共鸣？所以我现在用的方式是：开场先问大家——你心中真正的财富是什么？

turns.en: What do you really value? And I bring that up because, you know, my parents who grew up during the Depression and then fought in World War II and so forth and never, never able to accumulate a lot and didn't invest in public markets.
turns.zh: 你最珍视的是什么？我提这个，是因为我父母在大萧条里长大，又打了二战，一辈子没能积攒多少，也不投公开市场。

turns.en: And they didn't live as well in retirement as they probably could have. Anyway, I think about them. I started talking about embracing uncertainty, which we've covered here.
turns.zh: 他们的退休生活本可以过得更好。说起他们，我总会想到这些。我会从拥抱不确定性讲起——这个我们节目里也聊到了。

turns.en: That's uncertainty that creates the opportunity. And then when my parents, their true wealth was family. Their goal in life was to raise a good family, which they did.
turns.zh: 正是不确定性创造了机会。而我父母，他们真正的财富是家庭。他们的人生目标是把子女培养好，他们做到了。

turns.en: They were spectacular. And I tell people, you know, look, they were wealthy. They just didn't have much money. And so there's a difference between wealth and having lots of money.
turns.zh: 他们非常了不起。我常跟人说：你看，他们很富有，只是没那么多钱。财富和有钱是两码事。

turns.en: Start with that and then we need to embrace uncertainty. So then when I summarized all this academic research that's been going on the last 60 years, I looked, it comes in two parts.
turns.zh: 先从这个谈起，然后我们要拥抱不确定性。我把过去 60 年的学术研究做了总结，它分为两部分。

turns.en: First, stocks and bonds, with 100 years of data supporting this, they behave like we hope they would. Stocks do better than bonds, you know, because they're riskier.
turns.zh: 第一，有 100 年数据支撑：股票和债券的表现，确实如我们所希望的那样。股票比债券好，因为它更有风险。

turns.en: And over the long haul, stocks do about 10% a year. Bonds do four and a half or five. That's uplifting. You should feel good about that. So there are no guarantees about the future, for sure.
turns.zh: 长期看股票大约年化 10%，债券四五个点。这是振奋人心的，你该为此感到踏实。当然，未来绝无保证。

turns.en: And, you know, I find they talk about guarantees all the time. People want guarantees, obviously, in life and in investing. You know, there are long times there aren't guarantees about the big issues.
turns.zh: 而且我发现人们整天把'保证'挂在嘴边。大家在人生和投资里都想要保证。可在重大问题上，很长时间里根本没有保证。

turns.en: And so kind of my view is people want to feel safe. And by safe and their personal lives, they don't necessarily mean nothing bad can happen to them.
turns.zh: 所以我的看法是：人们想要的是安全感。而生活里的安全，未必是指坏事不会落到自己头上。

turns.en: I think it usually means something like, regardless of what happens, I'm going to be okay. I feel like I'm going to be okay. If you can feel like that in your personal life, then kind of feel safe.
turns.zh: 它更像——无论发生什么，我都会没事——的感觉。如果你在个人生活里能有这种感觉，那就是感到安全。

turns.en: And I think the same thing applies in investing. If people understood better how markets work, then they could relax a bit and feel safe, stay calm.
turns.zh: 我想投资也一样。如果人们更了解市场如何运作，就能放松一点，感到安全，保持冷静。

turns.en: And so, you know, once again, kind of draw a parallel between people's personal lives and investing. Parallels are really strong, I think. David, I want to start to weave together some of these threads that we've picked up on.
turns.zh: 所以你看，又一次，个人生活与投资之间形成对照。这种平行关系我觉得特别强烈。——David，我想开始把今天我们捡起的几条线索串起来。

turns.en: We've mentioned already the efficient markets hypothesis or EMH in passing. And I think you rightly share that, you know, no one's got a monopoly on language, though I think what we find in going back to our mark you made earlier is that, you know, I think many investors to this day may still feel like they're on the outside looking in.
turns.zh: 我们已经顺带提到了有效市场假说，EMH。你也说得对，没人垄断措辞权。但回头看我们前面的对话，我想今天仍有很多投资者觉得自己是局外人，在门外张望。

turns.en: So in an effort to bring more people in, I'm wondering if you could explain the basics of the efficient market hypothesis to our audience, either that needed a dust-up or otherwise just uninitiated.
turns.zh: 所以，为了把更多人带进'局内'，你能不能给我们的听众讲讲有效市场假说的基础？无论是需要重新温习的人，还是完全没接触过的人。

turns.en: Like, what does EMH mean in plain English and why does it still matter so much when we think about more broadly the science of investing today?
turns.zh: 用大白话说，EMH 到底是什么意思？当我们更宽泛地思考今天的投资科学时，为什么它依然如此重要？

turns.en: Well, basically it says that probably people can't outguess the market. The market does a great job of setting prices using Fama's language.
turns.zh: 嗯，它基本是说：人大概率猜不过市场。市场在定价上做得非常好。用 Fama 的话讲，

turns.en: It reflects all available information. So that's kind of a statement of it. And the first part of it, the other part is you don't have to try to outguess the market in order to have a good experience.
turns.zh: 价格反映了所有可得信息。这是它的表述之一。另一半含义是：你不必猜过市场，也能拥有很好的体验。

turns.en: In some ways, that's the bigger message. You know, markets work like we hoped they would and you can buy market portfolios easily. So you don't have to try to outguess the market.
turns.zh: 某种程度上，那才是更大的信息。市场如我们所愿地运转，而你可以很轻松地买到市场组合，所以你不必去和市场斗智猜涨跌。

turns.en: You can sit back and let markets work for you. I mean, the markets are where buyers and sellers come together. And people don't trade unless each side thinks they got a good deal.
turns.zh: 你可以坐下来，让市场替你工作。市场是买卖双方汇聚的地方，而每一方不会轻易交易——不觉得自己得了好买卖，谁也不会成交。

turns.en: And I think largely in stock and bond markets, a big institutional investor is they're really setting prices. You know, if institutions perceive prices deviate a little bit from fair price, they jump in all over that on one side or the other.
turns.zh: 我认为在股债市场里，真正在定价的是大型机构投资者。机构一旦发现价格略偏离公允，立刻就会从这一侧或那一侧扑上来。

turns.en: So you have these big powerhouses duking it out, each with access to similar information and so forth. And that kind of environment, what should pop out are fair prices.
turns.zh: 所以是一群巨头在互相角力，每一方都能拿到相似的信息。这样的环境里，应该浮现出来的就是公平价格。

turns.en: And that seems to be the case. If you look at market prices, the efficient market says they are where they should be. Markets aren't perfect, but people don't seem to be able to do better than that.
turns.zh: 看起来也确实如此。看市场价格，有效市场假说说它们就在该在的位置。市场不完美，但人们似乎也做不过它。

turns.en: They try to outguess the market and generating a lot of costs. And I would argue generate a lot of anxiety that's unnecessary. So the implication is there are straightforward ways to invest, for you don't have to do all the things you thought you had to do in order to have a good experience.
turns.zh: 人们试图猜过市场，付出大量成本，我认为还制造了大量不必要的焦虑。所以含义是：有直截了当的投资方式——你不必做你以为非做不可的那些事，也能有不错的体验。

turns.en: So if markets are generally efficient, what does that imply about the role and limitations of actively managed funds? Do you think the average investor should generally avoid active funds?
turns.zh: 那么，如果市场大体有效，这对主动管理基金的角色与局限意味着什么？你觉得普通投资者是否一般应该避开主动基金？

turns.en: Or do you think there's still a role for them maybe as a smaller percentage of a portfolio? I think you're under something there with a smaller percentage.
turns.zh: 还是说它们仍有一席之地，比如作为组合里较小的一部分？——你'较小比例'这个说法很到位。

turns.en: I've been around long enough to realize people are people. I mean, they get attracted to all kinds of wild ideas and strategies and ways to do better.
turns.zh: 我在这个行业够久了，深知人就是人。大家会被各种天马行空的想法、策略和'更高明'的门道吸引。

turns.en: So I've learned to say, OK, let's take 10 or 20% of your portfolio and you can do with it. Call it mad money, invest in it, and all these crazy ideas that you seem to be enamored with.
turns.zh: 所以我学会了说：好，我们拿出 10% 或 20% 的资金随你折腾，就叫它'疯狂资金'吧，去投你着迷的那些点子。

turns.en: But let's make sure 80% or 90% of the money here is invested in a sensible, long-term way. Rather than argue with people that they say, well, I'm really intrigued by this or that.
turns.zh: 但要确保 80% 或 90% 的钱，按合理的长期方式来投。与其跟人争辩'我真的很心动这个那个'，

turns.en: I go, OK, well, it doesn't float my boat, but let's make sure we stick to what the evidence from the science tells us. You know, we kind of stress that our approach is really based on kind of scientifically based hope.
turns.zh: 我不如说：行，那玩意儿不让我心动，但我们得守住科学证据告诉我们的东西。我们常说，我们的方法建立在'有科学依据的希望'之上。

turns.en: I would characterize it. You know, without the science, hope really just kind of becomes a wish. So that's the transformation. If you would like to have a good investment experience and then based on the science, there's no reason why you shouldn't have the expectation of having a good experience.
turns.zh: 我会这么形容：没有科学，希望就不过是一种许愿。这就是那个转变。如果你想要一个好的投资体验，那么基于科学，你没有理由不期待一个好体验。

turns.en: And if you want to gamble a little bit on, I mean, all this stuff and predictive markets and all of that. You know, I know what the long-term outcome of that sort of thing is going to be, but I'm not going to waste my time trying to convince people they have a negative expected outcome engaging in those markets.
turns.zh: 如果你偏要在预测市场之类的东西上赌一把——我心里清楚那类事长期下来是什么结果，但我不会费神去劝大家：参与那种市场，期望值是负的。

turns.en: As a financial advisor, you've got your clients back and we've got yours. With Vanguard's actively managed bond funds, you're backed by consistent performance with a low cost edge for an advantage that keeps compounding and compounding and compounding and...
turns.zh: 作为财务顾问，你的身后是客户，我们的身后也是客户。Vanguard 主动管理债券基金，以稳健的业绩和低成本的优势为你护航，让优势不断复利、复利、再复利……

turns.en: Sorry, quick break for legal. To learn more, visit vanguard.com.au. All investing is subject to risk. Investments and bonds are subject to interest rate, credit and inflation risk Vanguard Marketing Corporation distributor.
turns.zh: 抱歉，插播一段法律免责声明。欲了解更多信息，请访问 vanguard.com.au。所有投资都存在风险。投资与债券面临利率风险、信用风险和通胀风险。Vanguard Marketing Corporation 为分销商。

turns.en: And compounding, and compounding, and compounding. Are you backed by institutional quality bond funds? Vanguard. So David, that I think leaves a lot of investors in a place where you choose to take a meal ticket for what is often described as the only free lunch in this business, which is just basic diversification.
turns.zh: 复利、复利、再复利。你身后是否有机构级的品质债券基金？Vanguard。David，我想这会让很多投资者处在这样一个位置：把饭碗寄托在常被称作本行业"唯一免费午餐"的东西上——也就是最基本的分散投资。

turns.en: I'm curious your thoughts and how they've evolved on diversification. I think this is timely because where we sit now in this particular moment in markets more broadly is a moment wherein many of the major market index that we look at look increasingly concentrated with respect to not just the percentage of these index portfolios that are comprised by a small handful of names, but the amount of earnings that those names are generating, the amount of incremental capex that those firms are pouring into the economy.
turns.zh: 我很好奇你对分散投资的看法，以及它是如何演变的。我觉得这个话题很应景，因为我们此刻所处的市场时点——很多主要市场指数越来越集中，不仅是一小把股票占指数组合的比重在升高，这些公司创造的盈利、以及它们向经济中投入的增量资本开支（capex）也在集中。

turns.en: Is there a risk that diversification just in its purest sense, just owning the basic market, is at risk of potentially disappointing investors?
turns.zh: 最纯粹意义上的分散投资——就是持有基本市场——是否存在让投资者失望的风险？

turns.en: Well, first off, I mean, I think those are legitimate concerns. It does suggest that you want to maybe focus a bit more on viewing stocks as being a global market rather than just US.
turns.zh: 首先，我认为这些都是合理的担忧。它确实提示你，不妨更多地把股票看作一个全球市场，而不仅仅是美国市场。

turns.en: So internationally, there isn't that concentration. So if you had half your money outside the US, then half of that problem goes away anyway.
turns.zh: 在国际市场上，并没有那种集中度。所以如果你把一半资金放在美国之外，那这个问题就先解决了一半。

turns.en: So there's not really a great answer to that. You know, it looks like the industry is going forward. There might be a lot of concentration because that's really where the great ideas seem to be concentrated in some narrow industries.
turns.zh: 所以这个问题没有特别好的答案。看起来行业会一直这样往前走，可能会有很高的集中度，因为好的想法似乎确实集中在少数几个狭窄的行业里。

turns.en: On the other hand, you know, personally, I am worried about some of that concentration. Our basic investment approach, we hold all those stocks.
turns.zh: 另一方面，就我个人而言，我的确对那种集中度有些担忧。我们基本的投资做法是持有所有那些股票。

turns.en: We have a tendency to hold them in smaller amounts than they represent in the index. But, you know, I don't know what the alternative is. You know, my guess is over the long haul, the markets will take care of that.
turns.zh: 我们倾向于以低于它们在指数中权重的金额持有它们。但我也不知道有什么替代方案。我猜从长期看，市场会自己解决这个问题。

turns.en: In other words, one of my favorite kind of examples is go back to the Gold Rush. You know, Gold Rush in California in the 19th century, you know, flurry of activity.
turns.zh: 换句话说，我最喜欢的一个例子就是回到淘金热。19 世纪加利福尼亚的淘金热，一片狂热。

turns.en: It opened up to the West really. But who made the big money? I mean, you could argue it was Levi's Trouse. So, point being with all these high tech firms and so forth, there'll be winners and losers on that for sure.
turns.zh: 它真正打开了西部。但谁赚了大钱？你可以说是 Levi Strauss。我的意思是，在这批高科技公司之中，肯定会有赢家和输家。

turns.en: And it's, I don't know, anybody can predict who the big winners will be and who the big losers will be. But there'll be big winners and losers.
turns.zh: 没人能预测谁是大赢家、谁是大输家，这我不知道。但一定会有大赢家和大输家。

turns.en: And the economy, I think the benefit on the economy will spread out and you'll see, you know, benefit in a lot of the areas outside of this tech.
turns.zh: 而对经济的益处，我认为会扩散开来，你会看到很多科技之外的领域同样受益。

turns.en: But for the time being, that's kind of the way the market's configured. And I think that's a classic example. I think certainly in that moment, though, it's not one that anyone here lived through.
turns.zh: 但至少眼下，市场就是这么配置的。我觉得这是个经典的例子。当然，那个时刻并不是我们今天在座任何人亲历过的。

turns.en: I think many would have expected the big winners would be holding gold nuggets and not wearing blue jeans. Yeah, being a product of the 60s, I can tell you that jeans are a big deal, a big part of life.
turns.zh: 我想很多人当时会以为，大赢家应该是手握金块的人，而不是穿蓝色牛仔裤的人。是啊，作为 60 年代的产物，我可以告诉你，牛仔裤是一件大事，是生活的重要部分。

turns.en: And still are today. And still are today, you know. Yeah. So, when you founded Diventional back in 1981, what problem were you trying to solve that indexing alone didn't fully address?
turns.zh: 今天也一样，今天依然是这样。那么，1981 年你创立 Dimensional 的时候，你想解决的是单纯指数化没能完全解决的什么问题？

turns.en: Well, let me kind of back up a little bit about kind of the firm now. And what our goal is and our mission is really to apply the science in a way that makes sense.
turns.zh: 让我稍微回溯一下公司如今的情况。我们的目标和使命，真正说来就是以讲得通的方式把科学应用到投资中。

turns.en: And let's go back even to the mid-60s, you know, when the research first started coming out about the dismal performance of professionally managed portfolios.
turns.zh: 甚至要回到 60 年代中期，那时候关于专业管理组合业绩惨淡的研究才刚刚发表。

turns.en: People go, well, if you can't, I'll guess the mark. What are you supposed to do? And I, you know, started working at Wells Fargo. I decided I didn't want to be a professor after all.
turns.zh: 人们就说，如果你猜不透市场，那该怎么办？我那时在 Wells Fargo 工作，最后决定我还是不想当教授。

turns.en: And I walked into Fama's office. I was working for Jean at the time and said, I'm going to leave. He goes, well, I have this guy in San Francisco.
turns.zh: 我走进 Fama 的办公室——我当时是给 Gene 打工的——我说我要离开了。他说，我有个学生在旧金山。

turns.en: He's one of my students. I'll give him a call. That was Mack McQuown. And Mack was running kind of the think tank at Wells Fargo and working on trying to apply quantitative methods to various parts of the bank.
turns.zh: 他要给对方打个电话，那个人就是 Mack McQuown。Mack 在 Wells Fargo 主管一个类似智库的部门，试图把量化方法应用到银行的各个部分。

turns.en: And in the investment area, he was, he had this group that I went to work with. And we had two outside consultants, Fisher Black and Myron Scholes, who were working with us on it.
turns.zh: 在投资这块，他有一个团队，我就去那个团队工作。我们请了两位外部顾问，Fischer Black 和 Myron Scholes，跟我们一起研究。

turns.en: And while they were working with us, they developed the Black Scholes option pricing model. I mean, you have to understand, this is a wild west of research.
turns.zh: 就在他们和我们合作期间，他们提出了 Black-Scholes 期权定价模型。你要知道，那是学术研究的狂野西部。

turns.en: I mean, it's new ideas are popping up, you know, all the time in a way that they haven't been for the last, you know, say 20 years or so. Anyway, what our group was working on is how can we form portfolios that can beat the market without trying to guess the market?
turns.zh: 新想法不断冒出来，是过去——比如说 20 年——从来没有过的景象。我们那组人研究的是：如何在不猜市场的前提下，构建能跑赢市场的组合？

turns.en: Because we don't think, you know, picking stocks has a positive value add. And so we came up with a strategy, the so-called Sampsonite strategy, which the idea was we can create a portfolio that has a higher beta than the market.
turns.zh: 因为我们认为选股并没有正向的超额价值。于是我们想出了一个策略，所谓 Samsonite 策略：构建一个 beta 高于市场的组合。

turns.en: And so it should outperform the market. I mean, it's a pretty naive idea. It was a equally weighted index type approach. And, you know, we were young and naive in those days.
turns.zh: 它理应跑赢市场。这个想法相当天真，本质上是等权指数的做法。我们那时候年轻又单纯。

turns.en: There wasn't anything wrong with the idea. It wasn't a big winner. But that's we're trying to figure out where does science take us? And then the trust department, the bank, and it must be some marketing genius, came along and said, what you really want to do is an S&P 500 index fund.
turns.zh: 想法本身没什么错，只是没成为大赢家。但那是我们在探索科学会把我们带向何处。后来银行的信托部门——肯定出自某位营销天才之手——进来说，你们真正该做的是一只标普 500（S&P 500）指数基金。

turns.en: And the trust department goes, yeah, that's it. And so they went down that path. And that turned out to be a huge winner. Yeah, that group got sold a couple of times.
turns.zh: 信托部门说，对，就是这个。于是他们走了那条路，结果成了巨大的赢家。是啊，那个团队后来被转手卖了几次。

turns.en: And now it's really the cornerstone of BlackRock and the Reisshares, that indexing group. So that was an idea that really took off. And we go, yeah, but as a scientist, I wouldn't want to have an index fund.
turns.zh: 现在它其实是 BlackRock 和 iShares 那块指数化业务的基石。所以那是个真正一飞冲天的想法。而我们就说，没错，但作为科学家，我不想做一只指数基金。

turns.en: I mean, I wouldn't throw it out either, but it's leaving something on the table. I mean, a couple of reasons why. Well, number one is if you have a constraint on yourself, I want to track this index from just basic economic theory constraints have a cost.
turns.zh: 我也不会完全否定它，但它有所放弃。原因有几个。第一，如果你给自己加一个约束——我要跟踪这只指数——那么最基本的经济学理论就告诉你，约束是有成本的。

turns.en: OK, and then the second part is, you know, if you are an index fund manager, you've got to trade at the same time. All the other index fund managers do when a new stock comes in or out of the index and trade at the same time.
turns.zh: 第二，如果你是指数基金经理，当有新股票纳入或剔除指数时，你必须和其他所有指数基金经理在同一时间交易。

turns.en: Everybody else was trading. Probably is not a good idea. So we went down the path and our group eventually got shut down. But we've reconstituted ourselves eventually into dimensional in 1981 with the help of these big academics that we've mentioned.
turns.zh: 大家都在同一时间交易，这可能不是好主意。我们走了另一条路。我们那个组最终被关停，但后来在几位前述大学者的帮助下，于 1981 年重组成了 Dimensional。

turns.en: And as dedicated the idea that we can engineer it on the construction side portfolio better than the index providers do out there. And then we're not going to try to have zero tracking here relative to our benchmark.
turns.zh: 我们坚信，在组合构建这一侧，我们可以比市场上的指数供应商做得更精细，而且我们不会追求相对基准的零跟踪误差。

turns.en: Well, we'll use a little bit of flexibility and trading. There are any number of things can happen to you. Suppose you have a list of stocks and the amount that you want to buy in each and you go to the marketplace.
turns.zh: 我们会在交易上留一点灵活性。可能影响你的因素有很多。比如你有一份股票清单和每只想买的数量，然后你去到市场。

turns.en: Well, you want to adapt to what's going on in the marketplace. Some trades are tougher than others. And you kind of want to load up on the easy trades and avoid the tough trades and you can do things very clever things on securities, lending, whatnot.
turns.zh: 你要适应市场当时的情形。有些交易难做，有些容易，你总想多做容易的交易、避开难的交易；你还可以在证券借贷这些事情上做一些很聪明的操作。

turns.en: It's the only number of all these things we can call a market mechanisms. If you pay attention to those details, you can add a basis point here or there.
turns.zh: 所有这些东西——我们称之为市场机制——数目繁多。如果你关注这些细节，就能在这里或那里加上一个基点。

turns.en: And over the long haul, if you can add 10 or 20 basis points or more to return after fees, then you've done a heck of a job. And so we avoided the indexing route.
turns.zh: 从长期看，如果你能在费后收益上加上 10 或 20 个基点甚至更多，那你就已经干得非常漂亮了。所以我们避开了纯指数化的路。

turns.en: We went down the I would call it applying the science route. Indexing is fine. I just I don't think that's an elegant solution to what we've learned from research.
turns.zh: 我们走的是我所说的"应用科学"之路。指数化没什么不好，我只是觉得那不是对我们从研究中所学到的东西的优雅解法。

turns.en: I know that puts me in a minority here, but whatever, you know, he asked my opinion. I'm giving you my opinion. So well, I want to be so bold as to ask you for another opinion, David, and this one goes to largely a semantic argument.
turns.zh: 我知道这让我不在多数派之列，但无所谓，你问我的看法，我就给你我的看法。那么 David，我想斗胆再请教你另一个看法，这个更多是一场语义之争。

turns.en: The approach that you've described and the dimensionals applied now for 45 years, would you typify that as being an active approach or a passive one?
turns.zh: 你描述的、Dimensional 已经应用了 45 年的这套方法，你会把它归为主动（active）还是被动（passive）？

turns.en: Well, for years, I call it passive, but then the FCC came out with a language on our ETFs. If you don't have zero tracking error, then you're an active ETF.
turns.zh: 多年来我都称它是被动的。但后来 SEC 针对 ETF 出了一个界定：如果你没有零跟踪误差，你就是主动 ETF。

turns.en: So now I'm an active ETF. Whatever the name is, you know, it's really trying to apply the science. You know, our kind of message is if you have a pension fund, you can't increase your pension benefits if you have zero tracking error.
turns.zh: 所以我现在是主动 ETF 了。不管名字叫什么，本质上是试图应用科学。我们传递的信息大致是：如果你有养老基金，零跟踪误差就没法提高你的养老金给付。

turns.en: If we can make you more money, then you can pay great pension benefits or whatever. I'll go back earlier. You said, look, markets are largely efficient.
turns.zh: 如果我们能帮你多赚点钱，你就能给付更好的养老金，诸如此类。倒回前面，你说过市场大体上是有效的。

turns.en: And how do we talk about that? And what I characterize it is there is, you know, evidence that markets aren't perfectly efficient. You can get examples here and there, all kinds of anecdotes.
turns.zh: 我们该怎么谈这件事？我的概括是：有证据表明市场并非完全有效，这里那里能找到例子，各种各样的轶事。

turns.en: I don't think they amount to a whole lot, but that suggests the markets may not be efficient here or there. And kind of my answer to that is, well, if there are any inefficiencies out there, that's what's in short supply.
turns.zh: 我不觉得那些能说明多少问题，但它提示市场也许在某些角落不是有效的。而我的回答是：如果真有低效存在，那才是稀缺品。

turns.en: And it's unrealistic to think that if a manager is clever enough to find those inefficiencies, they wouldn't just raise their fees to the point where they capture all the vigorish instead of passing it on to their clients.
turns.zh: 如果一个经理聪明到能找到那些低效，他难道不会把费率提高到把全部抽头（vigorish）都赚走、而不留给客户吗？指望不这样是不现实的。

turns.en: I mean, look at that's the history of people with great long term track records. I mean, they have a tendency to keep raising their fees until the pain is too great, right?
turns.zh: 看看那些有长期卓越业绩记录的人的历史就知道了——他们倾向于不断提价，直到代价大到无法承受，对吧？

turns.en: So the implication of that is for your average investor, don't worry about it. There are some people out there that can kind of do better. It's unlikely you're going to participate in that because if somebody's got the juice, they're probably not going to share it with you as the way I characterize it.
turns.zh: 这对普通投资者的含义是：别操心这件事。确实有些人能做得更好，但你不太可能参与其中，因为按我的说法，如果谁真有两下子，他大概不会跟你分享。

turns.en: One follow up on some of these sort of science based research derived inefficiencies that you've discovered and tried to exploit over the years, things like size, value, and more recently, direct profitability.
turns.zh: 再追问一个关于你们多年来发现并试图利用的那些基于科学研究的低效问题，比如规模（size）、价值（value），以及更近一些的盈利（profitability）。

turns.en: How should investors think about what are often called factors or these dimensions of expected returns without over complicating things or feeling like they're like reading the driver's manual to a Klingon spaceship?
turns.zh: 投资者该如何看待这些常被称为因子（factors）或预期收益维度的东西，而又不把事情过度复杂化、不觉得是在读克林贡飞船的驾驶手册？

turns.en: Well, I think the way to think about it is kind of the first stop in thinking about investing in stocks is, okay, let's look at the overall market.
turns.zh: 我认为正确的思路是：投资股票的第一站，是先看看整个市场。

turns.en: So I'll start there. I'll just buy the plain market. If I have enough money to buy one percent of all the stocks, I'll buy one percent of everything.
turns.zh: 我从那里开始，就直接买市场组合。如果我有足够的钱买下每只股票各 1%，我就每样买 1%。

turns.en: And that causes you to put more money in the larger companies and less in the smaller companies, but you have the same overall ownership percentage.
turns.zh: 这样你就把更多资金放进大公司、更少放进小公司，但你对整个市场的持股比例不变。

turns.en: Then you look at the research. And the research, as you point out, suggests that smaller stocks have higher average returns and bigger companies and lower price stocks have higher average returns.
turns.zh: 然后你去看研究。正如你指出的，研究表明小盘股比大盘公司有更高的平均收益，低价股也有更高的平均收益。

turns.en: And then that's where you kind of got to get into how confident are you in that? You know, these findings cover long periods of time. There can be long periods of time when they don't work the way we hope they would.
turns.zh: 接下来就要看你对这些结论有多大信心了。这些发现覆盖很长的时期，但也可能有很长的时期它们不像我们期望的那样起作用。

turns.en: In fact, our first nine years went largely, you know, almost everything we had. It was US small cap. We started to be a name of a turbo run for small cap.
turns.zh: 事实上，我们的头九年里，几乎把一切都押在了美股小盘上，也因此眼看就成了小盘狂飙行情的代名词。

turns.en: So the first nine years we underperformed large cap stocks by quite a bit, our funds did. Well, the last 35 years have been great. So overall, it's done well.
turns.zh: 所以头九年，我们的基金比大盘股落后不少。而最近 35 年表现很棒，所以总体做得不错。

turns.en: But the point is, if you were an investor in that first nine years, when our returns looked pretty ugly, not everybody was able to stay invested.
turns.zh: 但要点是，如果你在第一九年——我们的收益看起来相当难看的时候——是投资者，并不是所有人都能坚持在场。

turns.en: And we lost a few clients along the way, as you might expect. But that shows the importance of not being overly confident about whatever the research ends up showing.
turns.zh: 一路上我们失去了一些客户，这你可以想见。但这正说明了不要对研究最终显示的结果过度自信的重要性。

turns.en: You know, one of the concerns you always have in looking at research is, is this really just due to the data mining or is this dimension or factor that we've observed?
turns.zh: 看研究时你始终要担心的一个问题是：这真的只是数据挖掘的结果吗？我们观察到的这个维度或因子是真实的吗？

turns.en: Is that really real? Can I really implement it? And those are complicated questions. So my answer to it is, as you start with the market, then you start leaning towards smaller companies or lower price stocks or higher direct profitability.
turns.zh: 它真的能落地实现吗？这些都是复杂的问题。所以我的回答是：从市场出发，然后向小公司、低价股或更高的盈利水平适度倾斜。

turns.en: That's a lot of gobbledygook. We have all of those options available to people so they can kind of decide for themselves. You know, I think, for example, small cap stocks, I think they have high-ravage returns because they're riskier and risk and return are related.
turns.zh: 听着像一堆天书。我们把这些选项都提供给了人们，让他们自己决定。比如，我认为小盘股有更高的平均收益，因为它们风险更大，而风险与收益是相关的。

turns.en: So other people might have different point of view. The data, I think, kind of makes me feel good about that. And we've observed long periods of time when that doesn't hold.
turns.zh: 别人可能有不同的观点。数据让我对这一点感觉比较踏实。而我们也观察过那些规律长期失效的时期。

turns.en: Gosh, one was a few years ago. We had like a 10-year run on the fang stocks and that caused people to get really attracted. Maybe there's magic here.
turns.zh: 天哪，前几年就是一例。FAANG 那批股票来了一波大约 10 年的行情，让人们特别着迷，想着这里面也许有魔法。

turns.en: If there's one thing I would try to suggest people keep in mind is there's no magic out there. We don't have any silver bullets. You know, investing and life is usually dealing with trade-offs rather than having optimal solutions.
turns.zh: 如果有一件事我想请大家记住，那就是：世上没有魔法，我们也没有什么银弹。投资和人生通常面对的是取舍，而不是最优解。

turns.en: David, I have a follow-up question for you more broadly in the vein of research. When you think about some of the original research, especially underpinning a dimensionals investment process, there's a moment where the raw materials of a lot of this were physical paper, pencils, and slide rules.
turns.zh: David，我想顺着研究的思路再问你一个更宏观的问题。回想支撑 Dimensional 投资流程的那些最早期的研究，当时的原材料其实是纸、铅笔和计算尺。

turns.en: And we fast-forward to today. And every day there's more data created in 24 hours than there had been in the whole of human history. Just raw computational horsepower we have at our fingertips is something we could have only dreamed of decades ago.
turns.zh: 快进到今天：每天 24 小时产生的数据比人类历史迄今的总和还多。我们指尖上的算力，是几十年前只能梦想的东西。

turns.en: What are the risks or opportunities there? And how do you see those manifesting to maybe unlock not pure magic, but another increment of magic that might be beneficial to investors?
turns.zh: 那里有什么风险或机会？你觉得它们会如何显现——也许不是纯粹的魔法，而是另一分对投资者有益的魔法？

turns.en: And do we also simultaneously have to have a much better filter than we ever have before? Because there's more apparent magic, things that don't hold up when they descend from the ivory towers of academia down to the mean streets of reality.
turns.zh: 我们是否同时需要比从前好得多的过滤器？因为表面上"魔法"更多了，而从学术象牙塔降到现实街头的过程中，很多东西是站不住的。

turns.en: Yeah, no, I think you're on to some theory. We have a lot more data than we ever had in the past, for sure. I don't know if we have a lot more meaningful information.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得你说到点子上了。我们确实拥有了比以往多得多的数据，但我不确定我们有了多得多的有意义的信息。

turns.en: So, you know, a few years ago we did a movie, actually, it ended up being an Errol Morris film called Tune Out the Noise, and we put it on YouTube.
turns.zh: 几年前我们其实拍过一部片子，最后是 Errol Morris 导演的电影，叫 Tune Out the Noise，我们把它放到了 YouTube 上。

turns.en: We had over 30 million views. So I'm encouraged by that in the sense that people are trying to say all this complexity is out there. How can I work through all that as an outsider and come up with something that's sensible?
turns.zh: 观看量超过 3000 万。这让我很受鼓舞，因为它说明人们在试图回答：外面有这么多复杂性，我一个局外人怎么把它理清楚，弄出个靠谱的东西？

turns.en: And here again, that's kind of why we wrote the book, too, is just make people feel comfortable. Yeah, things are probably more complex than they were, and clearly people only have to be able to think more critically than they've been required to do in the past.
turns.zh: 这也正是我们写这本书的原因之一——让大家安心。事情也许确实更复杂了，显然人们需要比过去更强的批判性思考能力。

turns.en: But it's not clear that complexity is adding a lot of value to people. I mean, are people happier now because we have a lot more information or they have more anxiety?
turns.zh: 但复杂性是否真的增添了价值并不确定。大家信息更多之后，是更快乐了，还是更焦虑了？

turns.en: I don't know. So, with that background of kind of constant news flow and market data and noise, how can investors tell the difference between information that's useful versus something that is distracting or even harmful?
turns.zh: 我不知道。那么，在这种持续不断的新闻流、市场数据和噪声的背景下，投资者如何区分有用的信息与干扰甚至有害的东西？

turns.en: Well, I think you've got to start with a point of view or an investment philosophy or something, grounded in science. So, we can start with just a simple idea.
turns.zh: 我认为你得先有一个观点或投资哲学，而且要扎根于科学。我们可以从一个简单的想法开始。

turns.en: I'm going to buy market portfolios for my equity to be global, or my market portfolio to mean just something that has hundreds or thousands of stocks in it and low turnover, low cost.
turns.zh: 我要买市场组合：股票部分要么是全球的，要么至少是包含成百上千只股票、低换手、低成本的那只组合。

turns.en: So, that's what I'm going to do. Start with that on the equity side and then a fixed income strategy that meets your needs. And then start to say, well, here's some alternative points of view that I want to consider.
turns.zh: 我就这么做。先从股票这一侧开始，然后配一个满足你需求的固收策略，再考虑一些其他可供参考的观点。

turns.en: You know, Bitcoin isn't in the stock indices and personally, I don't know a little bit. A lot of people are enamored with that. Okay, well, so you pay attention to what's going on.
turns.zh: 比如比特币不在股票指数里，我个人对它了解有限，很多人对它很着迷。好吧，那就留意正在发生什么。

turns.en: And if you see some things that appeal to you, I would say you want to always be able to adapt and experiment a little bit on the margin, find out what really works best for you.
turns.zh: 如果你看到一些吸引你的东西，我的建议是始终要在边际上保持适应和实验的能力，找出真正最适合你的东西。

turns.en: And if you experiment with things and they seem to work well for you, maybe you want to add more to it. And if they don't work so well for you, maybe you want to give up on them.
turns.zh: 如果你尝试了一些方法并且效果不错，也许你想加大投入；如果效果不好，也许就该收手。

turns.en: But if you start with it, I like to start with a solution that undoubtedly makes sense. Let's say you end up putting half your money into an equity market and half the money in the fixed income. It can't go too wrong without, I don't think.
turns.zh: 但你要从一个毋庸置疑合理的方案开始。比方说，你把一半的钱放进股票市场，一半放进固收，我觉得这样不会出大错。

turns.en: But it leads into one other question. Sometimes when we try to explain things simply, we end up sounding simplistic. Everybody has a serious financial issue.
turns.zh: 这也引出另一个问题。有时候我们试着把事情讲简单，结果听起来像过于简单化。每个人都有严肃的财务问题。

turns.en: No matter how much money you have. Eventually, even if you have a lot, you have estate planning and all kinds of issues. So the financial side is complex.
turns.zh: 无论你有多少钱。最终哪怕你很有钱，也有遗产规划等各种各样的问题，所以财务这一侧是复杂的。

turns.en: And what amazes me is people when they have a serious medical issue, they go to a doctor. And we all have serious financial issue. I think what you want to do is find out where you can get good advice or help in making a decision.
turns.zh: 让我惊讶的是，人们有了严重的健康问题会去看医生，而我们都会有严重的财务问题。我认为你要做的是找到在哪里能获得好的建议或决策帮助。

turns.en: I mean, whether it's data and software that you folks provide and Morningstar provides, or if it's talking directly to a financial advisor, I think people need help.
turns.zh: 不管是你们提供的数据和软件、Morningstar 提供的数据，还是直接和财务顾问谈，我觉得人们需要帮助。

turns.en: So I wouldn't, when approaching the problem, what do you do? I wouldn't try to do it all on my own. I think that's an all-important point, David.
turns.zh: 所以在面对问题时，我不会什么都自己干。我想我不会独自包办一切——David，我认为这是一个至关重要的观点。

turns.en: And I don't know if it was you that first said it, but personally, anecdotally, I remember once upon a time hearing you first say that the bottom of all of these numbers, all of this data, all of this money is people and people who need to ultimately trust the people that they're entrusting their wealth with, which is fundamental and is, at least in my book, which I'll never write, not going to change anytime soon.
turns.zh: 我不确定这话最初是不是你说的，但我个人记得，很久以前第一次听你说过：所有这些数字、这些数据、这些钱的底层，是人，是需要信任自己财富托付对象的人。这是根本性的，至少在我那本永远不会写的书里，这一点短期内不会改变。

turns.en: Right. Well, I think that's right. I mean, the first point I guess I'm making is, I think you can trust the stock and bond markets. And I think you can find trusted advice, whether it's a Morningstar or a financial advisor or whatever. And there's a lot of people out there you can't trust.
turns.zh: 说得对。我想我表达的第一点是：我认为你可以信任股票市场和债券市场，也可以找到值得信赖的建议，无论是 Morningstar、财务顾问还是别的什么。但外面也有很多你不能信任的人和不能信任的建议。

turns.en: And there's a lot of advice you can't trust. So be careful about all of that. But at the end of the day, I tell our employees, providing investment solutions is our business, and trust is our product. I mean, that's the bottom line.
turns.zh: 所以对这些都要小心。但说到底，我常跟我们的员工说：提供投资解决方案是我们的业务，信任才是我们的产品。这就是底线。

turns.en: So you got to find, and here you're going back to creating the book, if people better understood how markets work to be able, better able to trust markets.
turns.zh: 所以你得去寻找。回到写这本书这件事上——如果人们能更好地理解市场如何运转，他们就能更好地信任市场。

turns.en: And with that, I think they can stay calm and feel safe. And David, the book is about much more than markets and investing in the science thereof.
turns.zh: 我认为这样一来，他们就能保持冷静、感到安心。David，这本书讲的远不止市场和其中的投资科学。

turns.en: How more broadly has the idea of just embracing uncertainty changed how you think, in turn, more broadly about just success in the broadest terms, wealth, and just fundamentally living a meaningful life? Well, it's meant an awful lot to me.
turns.zh: 更广泛地说，"拥抱不确定性"这个理念如何改变了你的思考方式——关于最广义的成功、财富，以及根本上如何过有意义的生活？这对我意义重大。

turns.en: You know, I studied econometrics at the University of Chicago, which is basically trying to apply math to economic data. And you know, any model of the economy, there's so much uncertainty in an economy. I don't know how anybody could forecast anything, but you study how to deal with uncertainty. And it took me a lot of years to really wake up and go, well, that's true in investing, which I studied at school. And it really applies to life as well.
turns.zh: 我在芝加哥大学学的是计量经济学（econometrics），基本上就是把数学应用到经济数据上。任何经济模型——经济里有太多不确定性，我不知道怎么可能有人能预测任何东西，但你学的就是如何应对不确定性。我花了很多年才真正醒悟：投资也是如此，我在学校学的那套东西，其实对生活同样适用。

turns.en: How do people make decisions? You know, in that regard, sometimes I say, you know, uncertainty is underrated. People call, don't you mean overrated? No, it's underrated, because that's what really creates the opportunity. It's been so much fun and so valuable to me personally, of learning how to deal with uncertainty. Because in some ways, what I'm finding for a wide range of decisions you have to make involving uncertainty,
turns.zh: 人们如何做决策？就这一点，我有时会说，不确定性被低估了。别人会问，你意思不是被高估吗？不，是被低估，因为那恰恰是机会的来源。学习如何应对不确定性，对我个人来说既有趣又有价值。因为在某种程度上，你要面对的涉及不确定性的大量决策——

turns.en: there are some kind of rules of thumb. One is plan, don't try to predict too much. The stuff that's predictable, those are easy decisions to deal with, is stuff that's not predictable, like the stock market. And so don't waste your time trying to predict the unpredictable.
turns.zh: 是有一些经验法则的。其一是规划，而不是过度预测。可预测的东西好办，难的是不可预测的东西，比如股票市场。所以别把时间浪费在预测不可预测的事情上。

turns.en: You've got to come up with a sensible plan for dealing with the market and so forth. But then you want to pay attention to what's going on, adapt to it, you know, look for new information and play for the long haul and come up with sensible solutions. And then at the end of it all, judge yourself by the quality of the decision you make and not the outcome. My outcomes are important, but when you're dealing with uncertainty, sometimes they end up being disappointing.
turns.zh: 你得拿出一个应对市场等问题的靠谱计划。然后留意正在发生什么，适应它，寻找新信息，放长线，给出稳妥的方案。而到最后，你要用决策的质量而不是结果来评判自己。结果固然重要，但在不确定性之下，结果有时令人失望。

turns.en: That's why they call it uncertainty. So, you know, that sounds like a lot of gobbledygook, but that ends up being ties in closely to my personal life process for dealing with uncertainty.
turns.zh: 所以才叫不确定性。这听起来像一堆天书，但这其实与我个人应对不确定性的生活准则紧密相连。

turns.en: I think that's a great reminder that you can only control the quality of your decision making and not necessarily the outcome. And if you make good decisions over the long haul, you probably life will turn out well for you, I think. Right. So before we wrap up, if people listening remember just one principle from your career and this book, what would it be?
turns.zh: 我想这是个很好的提醒：你只能控制决策的质量，而不能必然控制结果；只要长期做出好的决策，你的人生大概会不错。那么，在结束之前——如果听众多只能记住你职业生涯和这本书里的一个原则，你会选哪个？

turns.en: Well, I think it's be optimistic about publicly traded stocks and bonds. They really work for you. Trust the markets. Stay calm and stay invested.
turns.zh: 我想是：对上市的股票和债券保持乐观，它们真的能为你所用。信任市场，保持冷静，长期在场。

turns.en: David, I think that's the absolute perfect note to finish on. We certainly won't put you on the spot and ask you to sing any Ava songs for us karaoke style. We have thoroughly enjoyed this conversation today. I've had a lot of fun with it too, and I've enjoyed working with you folks over the years.
turns.zh: David，我想这是再完美不过的收尾了。我们当然不会逼你现场来一段 ABBA 歌曲的卡拉 OK。我们今天非常享受这次对话。我也玩得很开心，这些年和你们的共事很愉快。
